subject: history_social
passage: In the 1720s and 1730s, Jai Singh II, the ruler of Jaipur in northwestern India, built several observatories, including one in his capital now known as the Jantar Mantar. Its instruments did not use telescopes; instead, they were giant structures of stone and brick, laid out to track the positions of the sun, moon, and stars. Their size served a purpose. On a larger instrument, each degree of the sky is spread over a longer distance, so observers could read positions more finely. The largest, a sundial nearly 27 meters tall, can show the local time to within a few seconds.
stem: According to the text, why were the instruments at the Jantar Mantar built so large?

choices.A: To make them visible to people throughout the city of Jaipur
choices.B: To allow observers to measure positions in the sky more precisely
choices.C: To hold the large telescopes used to track the sun, moon, and stars
choices.D: To show that Jaipur's observatory was grander than Jai Singh's others

explanation.why: The text says the instruments' "size served a purpose": on a larger instrument, "each degree of the sky is spread over a longer distance, so observers could read positions more finely." The size was meant to make measurements more precise.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says the instruments were meant to be seen across the city.
explanation.B: Correct. The text explains that larger instruments spread each degree over a longer distance, allowing finer readings.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the instruments "did not use telescopes."
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text mentions other observatories but never compares their size or grandeur.
